title: What are covariance and contravariance in C# generics?
description: in/out variance annotations, safe upcasts through generic interfaces, and why delegates flip the direction.

data.text: **Question:** What are covariance and contravariance in C# generics?

Variance lets a generic type built from a **more derived** type be used where a **less derived** type is expected — safely. **Covariant** (`out T`) allows the type parameter only in output positions: `IEnumerable<Derived>` converts to `IEnumerable<Base>` (you read Derived objects as Base). **Contravariant** (`in T`) allows it only in input positions: `Action<Base>` converts to `Action<Derived>` (something that can handle any Base can certainly handle a Derived). The `out`/`in` annotations on the interface/delegate definition are the compiler's safety contract — misusing the parameter in the wrong position is a compile error.

**Covariance (out) — 'produces T':**
- `IEnumerable<out T>`, `IReadOnlyList<out T>`, `Task<out T>`, `Func<..., out TResult>`
- Reading only: `IEnumerable<Dog>` IS-A `IEnumerable<Animal>` — every dog is an animal, so a stream of dogs can be consumed as a stream of animals
- Enabled since C# 4 for interfaces/delegates; arrays have always been covariant (unsafely — see the trap)
- The type argument appears only in return positions; putting it in an input position breaks the guarantee

**Contravariance (in) — 'consumes T':**
- `IComparer<in T>`, `Action<in T>`, `in T` parameters of delegate types, `IEqualityComparer<in T>`
- Writing only: `Action<Animal>` IS-A `Action<Dog>` — a handler that accepts any animal can be handed a dog
- Direction feels inverted because the relationship of the *container* flips relative to T

**The safety rule:**
- `out` = write-only to the outside (produce); `in` = read-only from the outside (consume) — from the *variable's* perspective
- The compiler enforces it: adding `in T` as a return type of an `out T` interface is a compile error — that's what makes the conversions sound

**The classic traps:**
- Arrays: `Dog[] dogs = ...; Animal[] animals = dogs; animals[0] = new Cat();` — compiles, throws ArrayTypeMismatchException at runtime. Generic interfaces don't have this hole — that's why `IList<T>` is invariant
- `List<Dog>` is NOT `List<Animal>` (List is invariant — it both produces and consumes T)
- `IEnumerable<Derived>` → `IEnumerable<Base>` works, but casting back and inserting a non-Dog fails (or is impossible through the interface)

data.title: Covariance and contravariance in real code

data.caption: Covariant types flow up the inheritance chain (Derived → Base); contravariant types flow down (Base → Derived) — both are safe because of the in/out position rules.

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- The out-produces / in-consumes mnemonic and which common interfaces are which
- Why List<T> is invariant while IEnumerable<T> is covariant
- The array covariance trap and why generics closed it
- Correct direction reasoning under pressure (Action<Base> as Action<Derived> — not the reverse)

items: Reversing the direction: Action<Base> converts to Action<Derived>, not the other way around
Expecting List<Derived> to convert to List<Base> — invariant because it both reads and writes T
Using array covariance in new code — it's a 1.x compatibility feature that fails at runtime
Confusing variance with inheritance of the generic type itself — IEnumerable<Dog> doesn't inherit from IEnumerable<Animal>
Forgetting that variance only applies to interfaces and delegates, not classes you define (annotate with in/out only on those)
Why can't your own class declarations use the in/out annotations?
Which is covariant, IComparer<T> or IEnumerable<T> — and how do you remember?
How does variance interact with generic constraints (where T : IFoo)?
Why is IReadOnlyList<out T> covariant but IList<T> not?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: out T (covariant): T only in output positions — IEnumerable<Dog> → IEnumerable<Animal>
in T (contravariant): T only in input positions — Action<Animal> → Action<Dog>
Interfaces and delegates only; the annotations are the compiler's safety proof
List<T> is invariant; arrays are unsoundly covariant — prefer generic interfaces
data.takeaway: Producers are covariant and consumers are contravariant — once that clicks, every in/out annotation and conversion question becomes a direction check.
